analysis.one_liner: Caps carbon dioxide emissions from new coal-fired power plants.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every new coal-fired power plant starting construction after April 2007 to limit its carbon dioxide output to 285 pounds per megawatt-hour — a level that in practice means plants would need to capture and store their carbon underground. The Environmental Protection Agency would have had to tighten the standard over time as better technology became proven. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to power-plant pollution, and communities facing climate-related harms like extreme heat, stronger storms, and rising seas, would benefit from fewer new long-lived coal plants built without carbon controls. The bill's own findings noted that over 150 new coal plants were proposed, which would have added roughly 500 million tons of carbon dioxide per year for the 50-year-plus lifetimes of the plants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near coal plants and the public

how_it_helps.text: New coal plants starting construction on or after April 26, 2007 would have had to meet a lifetime limit of 285 pounds of carbon dioxide per megawatt-hour, effectively requiring carbon capture and storage for conventional coal plants.
The EPA would have had to tighten the limit every five years starting by 2012 whenever better demonstrated technology made lower emissions achievable.
Carbon dioxide captured and injected into underground geological formations would not count as emissions, giving utilities a clear compliance path rather than forcing plants offline.

analysis.who_pays: Utilities planning new conventional coal plants and their investors would bear the cost of adding carbon capture technology or switching to cleaner designs, costs likely passed to electricity customers in coal-reliant regions. Coal mining interests would face reduced demand for coal if fewer new conventional plants were built.

drawbacks.text: Requiring carbon capture on new plants raises construction and operating costs, which utilities would likely pass on to electricity customers, particularly in coal-dependent regions.
The bill regulated only new plants; all existing coal-fired plants, which made up the bulk of power-sector emissions at roughly 30 percent of U.S. carbon dioxide output, would have been untouched.
Critics could argue the standard was set ahead of what capture technology could affordably deliver at scale in 2007, potentially deterring plant construction rather than cleaning it up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and climate benefits of preventing 150-plus new conventional coal plants — each operating 50 years or more — are large and long-lasting. The costs fall on utilities and ratepayers in coal-heavy regions, and the bill's own text acknowledges cost concerns by crediting captured carbon and requiring only proven technology for tightening the standard. The main design weakness is that it left existing plants unregulated, so its effect depended on the wave of proposed new plants actually being built.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kerry introduced the bill on April 26, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No further action was recorded: no committee markup, no floor vote, and no companion House action appears in the action history before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill had no cosponsors at any point during the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Utilities and coal interests planning new conventional coal-fired plants were better off, since the proposed 150-plus new plants faced no federal carbon limit. The communities that would have lived near those plants and the public facing climate harms lost the chance at tighter controls.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities and coal interests planning new plants

for.name: Sen. John Kerry
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired in the 110th Congress by Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or reported it out, keeping it from a Senate floor vote.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: The bill drew no Republican cosponsors, and carbon limits on coal plants had broad Republican opposition during this period.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors of either party; the bill never attracted cross-party support or a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would have forced any new coal plant to capture its carbon dioxide or miss the emissions cap, raising the cost of the 150-plus new plants then proposed. The utilities' interest in building cheaper conventional plants ran directly against the pollution limits the bill sought.

Carbon limits on new plants would reduce future demand for coal in electricity generation. Cheaper alternatives like natural gas and renewables would gain share if conventional coal plants were constrained.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and geological storage technology firms
industries.note: The bill created a compliance market by counting underground carbon injection as non-emissions, making capture and storage the main way new coal plants could meet the standard.
